characterList.description: A woman with medium-length brown hair, wearing glasses and a blue jacket. She is a counselor in Southwark and the cabinet member for Regeneration.
characterList.name: Fiona Collely

content_metadata.description: A video discussion about the regeneration project at Elephant and Castle, focusing on the vision and challenges involved from the perspective of Fiona Collely.

qAndA.answer: The tallest building shown is the Strata building.
qAndA.question: What is the name of the tallest building shown in the video?

qAndA.answer: Fiona explains that the Haygate Estate’s homes were not built to last and have become costly to maintain, with failing heating systems and power outages.
qAndA.question: Why is the Haygate Estate being demolished?

qAndA.answer: The council plans to build new homes on the Haygate Estate site, including affordable housing options and a mix of tenures, such as shared ownership and social rented housing.
qAndA.question: What is the council's plan to address the housing shortage?

qAndA.answer: There are concerns that international investors may drive up housing prices, making them unaffordable for local residents.
qAndA.question: What are the concerns regarding the involvement of international investors?

qAndA.answer: Fiona mentions the creation of a new park, the largest new Central London park in 70 years, and the preservation of mature trees.
qAndA.question: What specific details are given about the sustainable aspects of the development?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: I'm Fiona Colley and I'm a counsellor in Southwick and I'm the Cabinet Member for Regeneration.
And we're stood here in the shadow of the start of building and behind us is the Hage
Estate.
But what's your overall vision for elephant castle?
What will people be seeing if they come here in five years time or ten years time?
Well for a start we hope it'll start to be somewhere that people want to come and visit
and to live and to shop and to work.
At the moment the area's got a bit of a reputation for being run down, a concrete jungle.
And we really want to see that change.
This is a central London location and it should be an area that people are proud to live
in.
In Southwick's housing waiting list is on a critical level with some people having to
wait seven years for a home.
In that context is it wise to demolish a very large counsellor estate with thousands of
affordable homes and replace it with what some would see as more kind of up market type
deliverments?
Well the challenges with the Hage Aid were that whether we rebuilt the area or whether
we continued to maintain its castle homes it was going to be extremely expensive either
way.
And the opportunity arose for us really to change the area as well as to live a new
affordable homes that are for much higher quality than the current Hage Aid.
The plans include not just the 625 plus new affordable homes on the Hage Aid site but
also about another 700 or more affordable homes in neighbouring areas.
So overall we will see an increase in affordable housing in the Alfa and Castle area albeit not
on this particular site but of course that's part of our plans as well.
We don't think it's a good thing that you have all affordable housing on one site and all
expensive homes on another site.
The new area behind us when it's rebuilt will be a mixture of private housing, shared
ownership housing and social rented housing so that you'll have a properly mixed community.
Some critics suggest that the new so-called affordable homes will be less affordable
than the existing council stuff so the new homes will be affordable to those with the
lower income.
Well that's certainly a challenge for us and I think many of them will be affordable
for people on very low incomes.
In South Oak we are opposing the government's plans to change the definition of affordable
housing.
Certainly the Conservative government is very keen that housing associations should be
able to charge up to 80% of market rent and we don't believe that's affordable for people.
We want to make sure that the new homes are being built at a mix of tenures so certainly
some homes that are being built at the kind of rents that are equivalent to current
council and housing association rents which are around 35% of private market rents as well
as some shared ownership homes because many people who are on middle incomes and low incomes
who want to own homes can't afford private ownership in London so it's important to make
sure we've got those sorts of homes as well and as well as the full outright ownership.
We still don't expect elephant castles going to be a tremendously expensive place to live
compared to say the riverside and the south bank or west you know west minster but so we
do think there's a need for a mixture of tenures on this area.
He said you hope elephant castles still won't be too expensive a place to live but if you
look at a lot of the marketing literature by some of the developers it's very much geared
towards international investors who want to buy to let so is there a risk that the international
market could push up the prices because they seem to sort of openly they're openly happy
that in their terms the London housing market suffers from a lack of supply and a high
demand.
The words they're not enough houses and too many people will live with them which is great
if you can afford to buy to rent so there's a problem that the international market will
make things unaffordable.
I mean I think it's important to remember that when those homes are built up by international
investors that doesn't necessarily mean that they aren't lived in by local people.
I mean the private rented sector is very important too because as you've said we've got 20,000
people on our waiting list we won't be able to house all of them and many of those people
will rely on the private rented sector in order to find somewhere to live so that is
an important sector although I would like to see the government take steps to regulate
that market to ensure we get reasonable rents and security of tenure in the private rented
sector as well as the social rented sector.
I think it's understandable really that big developers will look overseas as well as
in the UK when they're trying to sell their properties off plan it is difficult for them
to get finance at the moment so they'll look to sell them wherever they can but I'm sure
we'll see plenty of local people, people on the learners and British people buying those
homes as well.
But if a local family was to rent a house off an international investor the chances are
it would be more expensive probably than say a council flat rented from the council.
Well I mean it would be but the family may or may not qualify for a council flat as you
said we've got 20,000 people on our waiting list even though we are one of the UK's
biggest social landlords so demand for housing certainly outstrips supply and not everyone
is going to be able to be housed by the council regardless of whether we knock down the
haggare or build the new homes or not.
We will see far more homes on this site than we have at the moment and clearly private
sector rents are set by the market and what people are willing to pay versus what people
supply there is and I don't think it makes very much difference whether people's private
sector landlord lives in the far east or lives in London.
The buy to let market is I'm sure here to stay and I would as I say like to see a bit more
regulation in the private rented sector to make that more stable and secure for people
but that is an important option for many people in London.
You've talked about the introduction of mixed tenure as opposed to a large council rented
development isn't the flip side of that the de placement of a large working class community
and some people seem to see this as gentrification and do you think that's a fair assessment?
No I don't think that is a fair assessment actually I think it's quite a naive assessment
in fact.
What we see increasingly on council estates because of the shortage of supply and because
of the rules around who gets the tough of the list is it's very rarely now working class
people and working people who get places on council estates so in fact what you I'm sad
to say you often get a council estates that are full of people who aren't working and
are on benefits although many of them are trying to get into work.
So I think having a mixed tenure area is much better certainly for kids growing up for
them to grow up in an area where there's a mixture of people, people who are working
as well as people who are out of work and I do think that's a much better environment
for everybody.
The developer claims that this is going to be a sustainable development but is it really
sustainable to knock down thousands of structurally sound homes only 35 years after the completion
and fail lots and lots of mature trees can that really be described as sustainable development?
Well we aren't failing lots and lots of mature trees actually in the latest version of
the Master Plan we're saving an awful lot from mature trees and that's a really important
thing that we were welcoming it was feedback from the public consultation that people wanted
us to do that.
We're creating a very large new park which is the largest new central London park for
70 years and I think the main lesson we have to learn from the homes that were built
35 years ago is that the homes we built in the future need to have a much longer lifespan.
These homes simply didn't turn out to be built to last.
They are structurally sound according to the Council's own survey so would there not
be a case for maybe refurbishing them because a lot of people have suggested that for
approximately half the hey gates life it didn't really have any adequate money on upkeep
spent on it.
I think that was certainly a problem in the 1980s but it was a problem that you will always
face when you have to keep rents low to keep them affordable that you aren't going to
have a lot of money for maintenance.
So they turned out to be high cost to maintain.
The heating systems were failing and needed replacing.
If you talk to people now who live on the elsewhere state you'll find that the vast majority
of them can't wait for those homes to be knocked down to have the new homes to move into
because the heating keeps breaking down.
I get emails every week telling me the heating is down again, the power's gone off, these
are not good quality homes and they are not homes that we can afford to maintain.
Having new high quality, sustainable, environmentally friendly homes is definitely the right way to go.
